topic.title: Factorising ax² + bx + c and more complex expressions (grouping, two variables)
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: A 2- to 3-mark Factorise early (Summer 2025 Q10, Summer 2026 Q14) and a 3-mark Factorise fully in the last third (Summer 2023 Q19, Summer 2024 Q18(a), November 2025 Q22(a), Summer 2026 Q17), the latter often carrying a 3-mark Hence simplify. Check by expanding the middle term only

note.title: Factorising ax² + bx + c and harder expressions
note.subject: maths

mustKnow: Pair with product ac and sum b, then split the middle term and group
Highest common factor includes letters as well as numbers
A perfect square trinomial: a² − 2ab + b² = (a − b)²

notOnThisSpec: Completing the square (excluded at M4 by the Teacher Guidance)
The factor theorem and cubics (A level, not GCSE)

mustBeAbleTo: Factorise ax² + bx + c by splitting the middle term with a pair whose product is ac and whose sum is b
Group four terms in pairs, choosing the sign of the second common factor so the brackets match
Take out the highest common factor first, numbers and letters together
Recognise a difference of two squares after a common factor, and finish the factorisation
Apply a² − b² when a or b is a fraction, such as 9/16 x² − 49
Apply a² − b² when a or b is a product of letters, such as 4x²y² − 9
Factorise a quadratic in two variables, keeping the second letter in both brackets
Recognise a perfect square trinomial such as 4p² − 20pq + 25q²
Use a factorisation in a Hence part: simplify an algebraic fraction, or find a missing side of a rectangle
sheet.howExamined: M4 (calculator, 2 hours, 100 marks). Two appearances. A short Factorise part early on, 2 to 3 marks, often as (a)(i) and (a)(ii) of a question whose later part solves an equation (Summer 2025 Q10, Summer 2026 Q14). Then a 3-mark Factorise fully in the last third, with a common factor containing a letter followed by a difference of two squares (Summer 2023 Q19, Summer 2024 Q18(a), November 2025 Q22(a), Summer 2026 Q17), sometimes followed by a Hence simplify part worth another 3. Schemes read MA1 for the common factor and MA2 for the completed factorisation, or MA1 for the split and A1 for the brackets.
traps: Looking for a pair that multiplies to c instead of ac when there is a number in front of x² (Summer 2024 M4 Q12(b), where wrong factorising produced impossible roots)
Taking out the common factor and stopping, leaving a difference of two squares unfactorised — most candidates in November 2025 M4 Q22
Taking out only part of the common factor: 3 instead of 3a, or 2 instead of 2n
Not recognising a fraction as a perfect square — most candidates scored zero on this case (Summer 2023 M4 Q19)
Dropping the second letter, writing (x + 5)(x − 3) for a quadratic in x and y (Summer 2023 M4 Q19)
Reading a perfect square trinomial as a difference of two squares, so both signs are not negative
Taking out +2 instead of −2 when grouping, so the two brackets do not match and nothing can be factorised
Cancelling single terms in a Hence simplify part instead of whole brackets (November 2025 M4 Q22)

Banking the mark for the common factor and going no further once three letters are in play: the bracket left behind is still a difference of two squares, so square-root each term as it stands, products of letters included (Summer 2024 M4 Q18)

Writing the letter first out of habit, so 25 − w² is factorised as (w + 5)(w − 5) — that is the negative of what you had; keep the two terms in the order the expression gives them (Summer 2025 M4 Q20)

noteBlocks.lede: Factorising runs expanding backwards: from $2x^2+9x+10$ back to the two brackets it came from. You already do it when the $x^2$ stands alone. A number in front of $x^2$ changes one thing, the pair of numbers you look for, and the rest is grouping, common factors and squares in disguise.
can: Split the middle term with a pair that multiplies to $ac$ and adds to $b$, then group.
Take out the highest common factor first, letters included, and finish every bracket.
Spot a difference of two squares in disguise: fractions, products, two letters, whole brackets.

noteBlocks.text: Multiply to ac, add to b

noteBlocks.alt: A two by two grid. The columns are headed 2x and +3, the rows x and +4. The cells hold 2x², +3x, +8x and +12; the corner cells 2x² and +12 are shaded.

noteBlocks.caption: The two middle cells, 3x and 8x, multiply to 24x²: the same as the shaded corners, 2x² × 12.

noteBlocks.md: For $x^2+7x+12$ you find two numbers that multiply to $12$ and add to $7$. With a number in front of $x^2$ the pair changes: for $ax^2+bx+c$ it must multiply to $ac$ and add to $b$. Split the middle term with that pair, then factorise the four terms in twos.
The grid shows why: its two middle cells always multiply to the same as its two corner cells.

steps.decision: Write ac down first: that single product is what changes when a is not 1.
List the factor pairs of 18 (1 and 18, 2 and 9, 3 and 6) and take the one that adds to 11.
Split 11x as 9x + 2x, then take a common factor from each pair. The two brackets match, which says the pair was right.
Take out the matching bracket. Check the middle: 3x × 3 = 9x and 2 × x = 2x, which add to 11x.

noteBlocks.title: Factorising quadratics 2
noteBlocks.why: The same split-and-group method on more quadratics with a number in front of x², at writing speed. Watch it once, then answer the checks without going back.

noteBlocks.explain: $ac$ is the $x^2$ coefficient times the constant: $2 \times 6 = 12$, as step 1 of See it multiplied $3 \times 6$. The pair you then want multiplies to $12$ and adds to $7$: $4$ and $3$.

twin.explain: $5 \times 6 = 30$; the pair then multiplies to $30$ and adds to $13$: $10$ and $3$.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which pair splits the middle term of $5x^2+17x+6$?
noteBlocks.explain: The pair multiplies to $ac = 5 \times 6 = 30$ and adds to $17$, as step 2 of See it listed the pairs of $18$: $15 \times 2 = 30$ and $15 + 2 = 17$. A pair built from $6$ alone ignores the $5$.

optionNotes.why: They multiply to 6, the constant, which is the rule only when there is no number in front of x². Here the pair must multiply to 5 × 6 = 30.
They do multiply to 30, but they add to 13, not 17. Both conditions have to hold: product ac and sum b.

twin.prompt: Which pair splits the middle term of $4x^2+13x+3$?
twin.explain: The pair multiplies to $4 \times 3 = 12$ and adds to $13$: $12$ and $1$.

optionNotes.why: They multiply to 3, the constant alone. With 4 in front of x² the pair must multiply to 4 × 3 = 12.
They multiply to 12 but add to 8, not 13; the pair needs both the product and the sum.

noteBlocks.text: Why the pair multiplies to ac

noteBlocks.alt: A two by two grid with columns headed qx and +n and rows headed px and +m. The cells hold pqx², pnx, mqx and mn; the corner cells pqx² and mn are shaded.

noteBlocks.caption: Corners multiply to pq × mn = ac; the middle cells pn and mq multiply to the same.

noteBlocks.title: The corners and the middle
noteBlocks.md: Expanding $(px+m)(qx+n)$ fills four cells: $pqx^2$, $pnx$, $mqx$ and $mn$. The corners give $a = pq$ and $c = mn$. The middle cells give $b$'s two pieces, $pn$ and $mq$, and $pn \times mq$ is the same four letters as $pq \times mn$. So the pieces of $b$ always multiply to $ac$.
The same grid is the quickest check on any answer: multiply the outer and the inner terms of your brackets and add; the total must be the middle term.

noteBlocks.stem: Show that the two pieces of the middle term of $(px+m)(qx+n)$ multiply to $ac$.

steps.decision: Multiply every term in one bracket by every term in the other: four cells of the grid.
Read off the coefficients: the middle term is made of two pieces.
The same four letters, multiplied in another order.

steps.working: So the pair that splits $b$ multiplies to $ac$.
steps.decision: That is why the rule works for every quadratic, and why c alone only works when a is 1.

noteBlocks.title: Why Splitting the Middle Works
noteBlocks.why: The same argument with the grid, spoken through. Watch it after the steps above, then try the check.

noteBlocks.prompt: $4x^2+8x+3 = (2x+1)(2x+3)$, and its middle term splits as $2x + 6x$. What do $2$ and $6$ multiply to?
noteBlocks.explain: The two pieces of the middle term multiply to $ac$, as step 3 of See it showed with letters: here $2 \times 6 = 12 = 4 \times 3$. They add to $b$, $8$; they multiply to $ac$, never to $c$ alone.

optionNotes.why: The constant is c alone, which is the product only when a is 1. Here a is 4, so the pieces multiply to 4 × 3 = 12.
8 is what the two pieces add to, not what they multiply to: 2 + 6 = 8 and 2 × 6 = 12.

twin.prompt: $6x^2+7x+2 = (2x+1)(3x+2)$, and its middle term splits as $4x + 3x$. What do $4$ and $3$ multiply to?
twin.explain: The pieces of the middle term multiply to $ac = 6 \times 2 = 12$ and add to $b = 7$.

optionNotes.why: The constant alone is the product only when there is no number in front of x²; here the pieces multiply to 6 × 2 = 12.
7 is the sum of the pieces, 4 + 3; their product is 12.

noteBlocks.text: Negative terms: let the pair carry the signs

noteBlocks.alt: A two by two grid with columns headed 3x and −5 and rows headed 2x and +3. The cells hold 6x², −10x, +9x and −15; the corner cells are shaded.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 214" width="300" height="214" role="img" font-family="system-ui, -apple-system, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Arial, sans-serif"><title>Area grid for (2x + 3)(3x − 5)</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"><rect x="78" y="44" width="104" height="70" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.09"/><rect x="182" y="44" width="104" height="70"/><rect x="78" y="114" width="104" height="70"/><rect x="182" y="114" width="104" height="70" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.09"/></g><g><text x="130" y="30" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">3x</text><text x="234" y="30" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">−5</text><text x="64" y="85" font-size="16" text-anchor="end" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2x</text><text x="64" y="155" font-size="16" text-anchor="end" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">+3</text><text x="130" y="85" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">6x²</text><text x="234" y="85" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">−10x</text><text x="130" y="155" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">+9x</text><text x="234" y="155" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">−15</text></g></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: A negative c makes one middle cell negative: −10x and +9x add to −x and multiply to −90x² = 6x² × (−15).

noteBlocks.md: When $c$ is negative, $ac$ is negative, so the pair has one negative number: look for two factors of $|ac|$ that differ by $b$. When $b$ is negative and $c$ positive, both numbers are negative.
Grouping then needs care: take a negative common factor from the second pair when that is what makes the two brackets match.

steps.working: $ac = 30$ and $b = -11$, so both numbers are negative: $-6$ and $-5$
steps.decision: Product +30 and sum −11: two negatives, from the pairs of 30.
Split −11x as −6x − 5x.
Taking −1 from the second pair, not +1, is what makes its bracket match (5x − 3).
Check the middle: 2x × (−3) + (−1) × 5x = −6x − 5x = −11x.

noteBlocks.prompt: The pair for $4x^2-4x-3$ multiplies to $-12$ and adds to $-4$. Which pair?
noteBlocks.explain: A negative product means one number is negative, and a negative sum means the larger one is: $-6 \times 2 = -12$ and $-6 + 2 = -4$, the sign rule step 1 of See it used.

optionNotes.why: The product is right, but 6 + (−2) = +4. The sum must be −4, so the larger number takes the minus sign.
They multiply to −3, the constant alone; the pair must multiply to ac = 4 × (−3) = −12.

twin.prompt: The pair for $3x^2+4x-4$ multiplies to $-12$ and adds to $4$. Which pair?
twin.explain: One number is negative, and the sum is positive, so the larger is positive: $6 \times (-2) = -12$ and $6 + (-2) = 4$.

optionNotes.why: The product is right but the sum is −4; the sum must be +4, so the larger number is the positive one.
They multiply to −4, the constant alone; the pair must multiply to 3 × (−4) = −12.

noteBlocks.md: Before looking for a pair, take out the highest common factor of every term, numbers and letters together. It makes the numbers smaller, and a factor left inside a bracket costs the last mark: "fully" means nothing more comes out of any bracket.
Letters count too: every term of $4ax^2+10ax+6a$ holds $2a$, so $2a$ comes out and the bracket left, $2x^2+5x+3$, is an ordinary quadratic.

steps.decision: 3 divides 6, 3 and 18, so it comes out first.
Work on the bracket with its own a, b and c.
Split and group inside the bracket; the 3 waits outside.
Keep the 3 in the final answer: it is part of the product.

noteBlocks.explain: Take out $2$ first, as step 1 of See it took out $3$: $2(2x^2+7x+6)$. Inside, the pair multiplies to $12$ and adds to $7$, $4$ and $3$, giving $2(2x+3)(x+2)$. A bracket with a common factor inside is not fully factorised.

optionNotes.why: It multiplies back correctly, but 4x + 6 still has a common factor of 2, so it is not fully factorised: take the 2 out.
Expand it: 2(2x² + 8x + 6) = 4x² + 16x + 12, not 14x. The pair inside must add to 7: 4 and 3.

twin.explain: Take out $3$: $3(2x^2+5x+3)$, then the pair $3$ and $2$ gives $3(2x+3)(x+1)$.

optionNotes.why: 6x + 9 still has a common factor of 3; take it out to finish.
Expanding gives 3(2x² + 7x + 3) = 6x² + 21x + 9, not 15x; check the middle term before you stop.

noteBlocks.text: A difference of two squares in disguise

noteBlocks.alt: On the left, a square of side a with a smaller square of side b cut from one corner, leaving an L-shape labelled a² − b². On the right, the same area rearranged as a rectangle a + b long and a − b wide, labelled (a + b)(a − b).

noteBlocks.md: $a^2-b^2=(a+b)(a-b)$ for any $a$ and $b$. After a common factor comes out, what is left is often a square minus a square with numbers in front: $9x^2 = (3x)^2$ and $4y^2 = (2y)^2$. A middle term means it is not a difference of two squares: $4x^2-12x+9$ is the square $(2x-3)^2$.

steps.decision: The highest common factor of 18 and 8 is 2; the letters share nothing.
Write each term as something squared: the bracket is a square minus a square.
Apply a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b), keeping the 2 outside.

noteBlocks.explain: Take out $3$, then $9p^2-4q^2$ is $(3p)^2-(2q)^2$, a difference of two squares, as step 2 of See it rewrote $9x^2-4y^2$. "Fully" means finishing it: $3(3p+2q)(3p-2q)$.

optionNotes.why: The common factor is right and earns its mark, but the bracket is still a square minus a square, so it is not fully factorised.
A squared bracket has a middle term when expanded, −12pq; this expression has none, so it is (3p + 2q)(3p − 2q).
The common factor is out, but the bracket is a difference of two squares that still factorises.
It multiplies back correctly, but 10m + 4n still has a factor of 2: take it out to finish.

noteBlocks.text: Fractions and products can be squares

noteBlocks.md: A fraction is a square when its top and bottom are: $\frac{9}{25}x^2 = \left(\frac{3}{5}x\right)^2$, because $\sqrt{9} = 3$ and $\sqrt{25} = 5$. A product of letters can be a square too: $16x^2y^2 = (4xy)^2$. Most candidates scored nothing on a fraction like this in Summer 2023, only because they did not look for the square root.

steps.decision: Square-root the top and the bottom of the fraction separately.
Apply a² − b² with a = 3x/5 and b = 2.

steps.working: Check: $\frac{3}{5}x \times \frac{3}{5}x = \frac{9}{25}x^2$ and the middle terms cancel
steps.decision: Expanding back is the fastest check that nothing was lost.

noteBlocks.explain: $\frac{1}{16}x^2 = \left(\frac{1}{4}x\right)^2$ because $\sqrt{1} = 1$ and $\sqrt{16} = 4$, the square root step 1 of See it took; and $9 = 3^2$. So it is $\left(\frac{1}{4}x+3\right)\left(\frac{1}{4}x-3\right)$.

optionNotes.why: Taking 1/16 out leaves x² − 144 inside, not x² − 9, so this does not multiply back to the question.
Its square term is x²/256, not x²/16: the fraction has to be square-rooted, top and bottom.
Taking 4/49 out changes the 1 inside: this multiplies back to 4x²/49 − 4/49, not the question.
The fraction was not square-rooted: its square is 16x²/2401, not 4x²/49.

noteBlocks.md: A quadratic in $x$ and $y$ factorises by the same pair: $ac$ and $b$ are the coefficients. The second letter stays beside each number in the brackets, or the $y^2$ term could not appear when you multiply back. Check a two-letter answer that way: the $x^2$, $xy$ and $y^2$ terms must all come back.

steps.decision: Use the coefficients 3, 7 and 2 exactly as in a one-letter quadratic.

noteBlocks.text: How the paper asks: factorise, then use it

noteBlocks.md: The command is bare: "Factorise" or "Factorise fully", 2 or 3 marks, the first for the common factor or the split and the last for the complete product. Every M4 paper from 2018 to 2026 has at least one, and the later one often continues: "Hence simplify" a fraction.

Four losses recur in the reports: stopping after the common factor (November 2025); dividing single terms instead of whole brackets (November 2024, 35% full marks); reordering a difference of two squares so a sign changes (Summer 2025); and missing a fraction's square root (Summer 2023).

Terms were cancelled one by one; only a whole bracket common to top and bottom can cancel.

noteBlocks.md: The hardest versions put a whole bracket where a letter would be: $(4n+3)^2-(3n+4)^2$ in Summer 2022, $(x-2)^2+5(x-2)$ in January 2019. findTheMistake.stem: Aoibhinn was asked to factorise fully $3ax^2 - 75ay^2$. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The common factor is exactly right, including the $a$. What is left inside the bracket, $x^2 - 25y^2$, is a difference of two squares, and the word **fully** means it has to be factorised too.
findTheMistake.feedback: One of the three marks is safe: taking out 3a, letters included, is the step many candidates miss altogether. The habit that collects the other two is to look at every bracket you write and ask whether it is still factorisable. November 2025 M4 Q22: most took 3a out, and only the top candidates saw the difference of two squares left behind.

findTheMistake.stem: Conor was asked to factorise $6x^2 - 5x - 6$. His working:
studentWorking: Need two numbers with product −6 and sum −5
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The pair was chosen to multiply to $c$, which is the rule only when the coefficient of $x^2$ is 1. Here $a = 6$, so the product needed is $ac = 6 \times (-6) = -36$, with sum $-5$: that is $4$ and $-9$.
findTheMistake.feedback: Notice that the grouping in line 4 was attempted properly — the method is sound, it was fed the wrong pair. Write $ac$ on the page before you hunt for numbers; the moment the two brackets fail to match, that is the signal the pair came from $c$ rather than $ac$. Summer 2024 M4 Q12(b): wrong factorising produced answers of 40 and 6 that could never have solved the equation.

findTheMistake.stem: Sorcha was asked to factorise $\dfrac{4}{25}x^2 - 9$. Her working:
studentWorking: So this is not a difference of two squares
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: A fraction can be a perfect square: square-root the numerator and the denominator separately. $\sqrt{4} = 2$ and $\sqrt{25} = 5$, so $\tfrac{4}{25}x^2 = \left(\tfrac{2}{5}x\right)^2$, and $9 = 3^2$.
correction: a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b) with a = 2x/5 and b = 3
findTheMistake.feedback: Nothing here is careless — it is a gap, and it is a common one: Summer 2023 M4 Q19 reported that most candidates scored zero on the fractional case. Add one line to your checklist: before deciding a difference will not factorise, take the square root of each term, fractions included, top and bottom separately.
